idiom_name: package per module; Scala 3 top-level definitions and export for the published surface
implementation_notes: A Scala package is a pure namespace on the JVM - nothing is enforced at run time - so the module's boundary comes from package-scoped visibility (private[billing]) plus the published surface you choose. In Scala 3 a package can hold top-level classes, functions and givens directly, without a wrapping object, and an export clause can publish selected internal members under the package's own names, which is the modern replacement for the package-object facade: export billing.internal.Pricing exposes exactly that member and nothing else.
pitfalls: Package-private is written private[pkg] and still leaks through companions, inheritance and generated accessors; the JVM has no notion of a package boundary at run time.
Wildcard exports from a package are forbidden, so a facade has to name what it publishes - convenient for documenting the interface, inconvenient when it is large.
Name resolution has binding precedence (local, then explicit import, then wildcard import, then package clause), so importing an internal name can silently shadow a package-level definition.

variants.name: Scala 2 package object as the package-wide surface
variants.idiom_name: package object (package.scala) as the package-wide published surface
variants.implementation_notes: In Scala 2 the package object is the only way to add package-level definitions and type aliases: package object billing in billing/package.scala exposes helpers and re-exports to the package and, as members of billing, to clients. It is the classic facade for a module whose implementation lives in sub-packages; Scala 3 deprecates the idiom in favour of top-level definitions and export clauses, so new code should prefer the Scala 3 form even when it must still compile for Scala 2 libraries.
pitfalls: Only one package object per package, so the published surface cannot be split across files once it grows.
Package objects are initialised eagerly per package and contribute members to clients' implicit scope, which can change resolution and startup behaviour.
